result: NuRD complex components (HDA-1, LIN-53, CHD-3, MEP-1) are asymmetrically segregated into surviving daughter cells during asymmetric cell divisions in C. elegans Q neuroblasts. This asymmetry develops progressively during anaphase through protein redistribution rather than new synthesis, reaching 1.5-1.8-fold enrichment in surviving cells by cytokinesis completion.
evaluation: Claims C1, C26-C34, C36-C38, C41-C42 provide converging evidence from live imaging of both overexpressed and endogenous tagged NuRD components showing asymmetric distribution. The timing data (C27, C34), quantitative measurements (C32-C33), and constant total fluorescence (C41) support the redistribution mechanism (C29, C42). Multiple cell lineages show consistent patterns (C37-C38).

result: Asymmetric NuRD segregation depends on PIG-1 kinase activity, as pig-1 mutants show symmetric distribution of HDA-1 and LIN-53 during asymmetric cell divisions.
evaluation: Claims C44-C45 are supported by fluorescence imaging data in pig-1 mutants showing loss of NuRD asymmetry (Figure 1—figure supplement 5, Videos 6-7). This establishes PIG-1 as an upstream regulator of NuRD asymmetry, consistent with its known role in asymmetric cell division.

result: NuRD asymmetric segregation occurs in multiple embryonic cell lineages that produce apoptotic daughters. In 15 of 17 embryonic ACDs producing apoptotic cells, surviving daughters showed >1.5-fold NuRD enrichment, with 6 reaching statistical significance.
evaluation: Claims C46-C47, C52 are supported by systematic quantitative analysis across embryonic lineages using automated cell tracking (Figure 2A-B, Supplementary file 2). The data demonstrate that NuRD asymmetry is a widespread phenomenon in C. elegans development, though not universal.

result: NuRD asymmetry does not universally predict apoptotic timing, as some cells with symmetric NuRD undergo rapid apoptosis while others with symmetric NuRD show delayed apoptosis, suggesting NuRD-independent mechanisms exist in certain lineages.
evaluation: Claims C48-C51 identify important exceptions to the NuRD-apoptosis relationship. The MSpppaa lineage (C48) and ABaraaaap lineage (C50) show that NuRD levels alone do not determine apoptotic fate in all contexts, supporting the inference of NuRD-independent mechanisms (C51).

result: Loss of NuRD function by RNAi increases apoptosis through the canonical EGL-1-CED-9-CED-4-CED-3 pathway. hda-1 RNAi increased apoptotic cells from 10 to 14 in ced-1 mutants, and this increase was suppressed in ced-3, ced-4, ced-9, and egl-1 mutants.
evaluation: Claims C2, C56-C59 are supported by quantitative apoptosis assays using the sAnxV::GFP reporter (Figure 3A-B). The genetic epistasis analysis with apoptosis pathway mutants (C58-C59) demonstrates that NuRD acts upstream of or through the canonical apoptosis pathway.

result: NuRD loss increases egl-1 expression through elevated H3K27 acetylation at the egl-1 locus. RNA-seq, RT-qPCR, and transcriptional reporter assays show increased egl-1 expression upon hda-1 or lin-53 RNAi, while ChIP-seq and ChIP-qPCR demonstrate specific H3K27ac enrichment at the egl-1 TSS and gene body.
evaluation: Claims C60-C67 provide multi-layered evidence linking NuRD to egl-1 regulation: transcriptional upregulation (C60-C62), increased promoter activity (C62), and specific chromatin changes at the egl-1 locus (C64-C66). The specificity is demonstrated by lack of changes in adjacent genes (C65). This mechanistically connects NuRD asymmetry to apoptosis.

result: Ectopic NuRD in apoptotic cells enables their survival. BafA1 treatment caused symmetric HDA-1 distribution without affecting cell size asymmetry, and 11/12 QR.aa cells with ectopic NuRD survived >120 min and formed neurite-like outgrowths. Auxin-mediated HDA-1 depletion restored apoptosis.
evaluation: Claims C3, C78-C84 demonstrate sufficiency of NuRD for cell survival through pharmacological manipulation (BafA1) and genetic rescue (auxin-inducible degradation). The specificity is shown by preserved cell size asymmetry (C79-C80) and restoration of apoptosis upon NuRD depletion (C83). This is strong evidence for NuRD's causal role in fate determination.

result: V-ATPase physically interacts with NuRD. Co-immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry identified 12 V-ATPase subunits binding to HDA-1::GFP, confirmed by western blot with anti-VHA-13 antibodies.
evaluation: Claims C4-C5, C68-C70 are supported by biochemical evidence (Figure 4A-C). The identification of 12 V-ATPase subunits (C68) is consistent with prior work identifying 4 subunits (C69), and the interaction is independently confirmed by western blot (C70). This establishes a physical link between NuRD and V-ATPase.

result: V-ATPase is asymmetrically segregated into surviving daughter cells during ACD, similar to NuRD. VHA-17::wrmScarlet showed enrichment in the surviving QR.ap portion.
evaluation: Claims C6, C85-C86 are supported by live imaging of VHA-17::wrmScarlet (Figure 6A-B, Video 10). The co-segregation pattern (C86) suggests coordinated distribution of V-ATPase and NuRD, consistent with their physical interaction.

result: Cytosolic pH becomes asymmetric during ACD, with the future apoptotic cell becoming more acidic. pHluorin fluorescence decreased in the anterior (apoptotic) portion but remained constant in the posterior (surviving) portion, with a 1.6-fold ratio that was reduced to 1.3-fold by BafA1 treatment.
evaluation: Claims C7, C73-C74, C76-C77 are supported by pHluorin imaging data (Figure 5A-B, Video 8). The interpretation that reduced fluorescence indicates acidification (C74) is reasonable given pHluorin's pH-sensitive properties. BafA1's effect (C76-C77) links V-ATPase activity to pH asymmetry, though the authors appropriately note the caveat about protein amount changes.

result: V-ATPase inhibition by BafA1 disrupts both NuRD and V-ATPase asymmetric distribution. BafA1 treatment resulted in symmetric HDA-1 segregation and disrupted VHA-17 asymmetry.
evaluation: Claims C8, C78, C87-C88 are supported by imaging data showing loss of asymmetry for both NuRD (Figure 5C-D) and V-ATPase (Figure 6A-B) upon BafA1 treatment. The inference that proton-pumping activity is important (C88) is reasonable but should be interpreted cautiously given BafA1's potential pleiotropic effects.

result: The authors propose a dual-function model where V-ATPase facilitates NuRD asymmetry through: (i) physical interaction and co-segregation, and (ii) generating pH asymmetry that contributes to asymmetric segregation.
evaluation: Claims C89, C93-C95 represent a proposed mechanistic model. While the physical interaction (C93) is well-supported, the causal role of pH asymmetry in driving segregation (C95) remains speculative. The model is consistent with the data but alternative mechanisms (e.g., pH-independent effects of V-ATPase) are not excluded. Further experiments directly manipulating pH would be needed to test this model.

result: V-ATPase colocalizes with the ER marker SP12 during ACDs, suggesting NuRD-V-ATPase may be delivered as cargo on ER or ER-derived vesicles.
evaluation: Claims C103-C104 are supported by colocalization data (Figure 4—figure supplement 2). The colocalization with ER (C103) is well-documented, though the inference about cargo delivery (C104) is speculative. This provides a potential mechanism for asymmetric distribution but requires further validation.

result: The authors propose that reduced NuRD in apoptotic daughters leads to increased H3K27ac at egl-1, resulting in egl-1 upregulation and apoptosis induction.
evaluation: Claims C90, C92 synthesize multiple lines of evidence into a mechanistic model. While each component is supported (NuRD asymmetry, H3K27ac changes, egl-1 upregulation, apoptosis), the direct causal chain in asymmetrically dividing cells is inferred rather than directly demonstrated. The model is well-supported but would benefit from cell-specific chromatin analysis.

result: The authors caution that transcript asymmetry detected by scRNA-seq may not correspond to protein asymmetry, as 6487/8624 genes were not detected in egl-1-positive cells, which may be undergoing apoptosis.
evaluation: Claims C96-C99 represent appropriate scientific caution about interpreting scRNA-seq data. The observation that most genes are not detected in egl-1+ cells (C97) supports the interpretation that these cells are degrading (C98). This is a valid limitation of the scRNA-seq approach for studying protein asymmetry.

result: The authors propose two potential mechanisms for NuRD asymmetry: (i) polarized microtubule-based transport of NuRD-V-ATPase organelles, and (ii) differential chromatin recruitment based on sister chromatid differences. The greater nuclear asymmetry (1.5-1.8-fold) compared to cellular asymmetry (1.3-fold) suggests both mechanisms may act together.
evaluation: Claims C106-C107, C109, C111 propose mechanistic hypotheses based on analogy to other systems and quantitative differences in asymmetry. While the differential asymmetry observation (C110) is data-supported, the proposed mechanisms (C106-C107) are speculative. The inference that both mechanisms act together (C111) is reasonable but requires direct experimental validation.

result: In divisions producing two surviving daughters, NuRD is equally distributed in 390/395 cases, but 5 cases showed significant HDA-1/LIN-53 differences, suggesting NuRD asymmetry may contribute to binary fate decisions beyond apoptosis.
evaluation: Claims C115-C117 are supported by systematic embryonic lineage analysis (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 2). The observation of rare asymmetry in non-apoptotic divisions (C116) is intriguing, though the inference about broader roles (C117) is speculative and would require functional validation.

result: Background claims establishing the biological context: ACDs produce daughters with identical DNA but distinct fates through extrinsic and intrinsic mechanisms; epigenetic mechanisms guide differential gene expression; C. elegans is a valuable model with 131 apoptotic cells, 105 from neuronal lineages including the tractable Q neuroblast system.
evaluation: Claims C11-C25 provide well-established background knowledge supported by appropriate citations. These contextual claims are accurate representations of the field and establish the rationale for the study. C. elegans developmental biology (C21-C25) is particularly well-documented.

result: Background claims about V-ATPase structure/function and epigenetic modifications: V-ATPase is a proton pump with V0 and V1 domains that regulates pH homeostasis and apoptosis; H3K27ac is associated with active gene expression; cytosolic acidification is a common apoptosis feature.
evaluation: Claims C71-C72, C75, C91 represent well-established knowledge supported by appropriate citations. These provide necessary context for interpreting the experimental findings and are accurately stated.

result: The authors identify knowledge gaps: little is known about asymmetric segregation of epigenetic modification enzymes during ACDs or the functions of polarized V-ATPase distribution and cytoplasmic proton asymmetry.
evaluation: Claims C100-C101 accurately characterize gaps in the field that this study addresses. These statements appropriately position the novelty of the work.
